title: US Immigrant Visas Halve to 26,483 as Restrictions Cover 91 Countries; India Down 16%
excerpt: February 2026 issuances fell to about half the pre-Trump monthly average of 52,000, with immigrant visas for Indians down 16% and employment-based categories the one route still holding steady.
body:
• The State Department issued 26,483 immigrant visas in February 2026, about half the monthly average of roughly 52,000 before President Trump's second term, per State Department monthly statistics reported by the New York Times.
  • Immigrant visas for Indian nationals fell 16%, with sharper drops for China (-31%), Japan (-25%) and South Korea (-19%); 91 countries now face travel or visa restrictions, and visa issuance from Muslim-majority nations has fallen more than 90%.
  • If you are an Indian applicant: India is not on any ban list, but consular processing is slower and immigrant visas for the country are down 16% — check the State Department's monthly immigrant visa statistics and the latest visa processing updates before filing or booking consular appointments.
  • Employment-based immigrant visas held nearly steady (3,264 in February 2026 vs. 3,287 two years earlier) — the collapse is concentrated in family reunification and the diversity lottery, which issued zero visas in January and February 2026.

The United States issued just 26,483 immigrant visas in February 2026, barely half the roughly 52,000-a-month average of the pre-Trump years, as sweeping visa restrictions reshaped who can legally enter the country. The numbers, drawn from the State Department's own monthly visa statistics and first reported by the New York Times, trace one of the sharpest contractions of legal immigration in modern American history.

The contraction did not arrive all at once. Visa issuances fell by roughly 10% during the first year after President Donald Trump's return to office, according to the New York Times analysis. It accelerated sharply in January 2026, when an expanded travel ban restricted entry and visa access for nationals of 39 countries while immigrant visa issuance was suspended for applicants from another 52. Between the bans, the suspensions and limits on Palestinian nationals, restrictions now touch applicants from 91 countries, with another 61 seeing immigrant visa availability reduced.

Which categories collapsed — and which didn't

The data reveal a highly uneven picture. Most immigrant visas go to relatives of U.S. citizens and green card holders, and those bore the brunt: visas for parents of U.S. citizens fell from 11,367 in February 2024 to 5,264 in February 2026, a 54% drop, while visas for spouses of U.S. citizens fell 27%, from 9,341 to 6,847, according to State Department tables. The diversity visa lottery — suspended effective December 23, 2025 — issued no visas at all in January or February 2026, down from 4,738 in February 2024.

Employment-based immigration, by contrast, held almost perfectly steady. Visas in the main employment-based classes numbered 3,264 in February 2026, compared with 3,287 two years earlier. The resilience of the green card track for employer-sponsored applicants matters most for Indian professionals, who dominate those categories — but it sits alongside a bleaker picture for temporary worker pathways.

"Monthly legal entries had actually fallen 2.7 times more than illegal entries through February 2026."

— David J. Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute

Temporary visas and students take the hit

The restrictions spilled well beyond immigrant visas. Student and worker visa issuances fell 30% year-on-year, while tourist and business visitor visas declined roughly 25% in February, the New York Times reported. A Cato Institute analysis by Bier found student visa issuances still down 42% as of February 2026 compared with February 2024, and H-1B visas along with H-4 visas for spouses and children down 78% from February 2024 levels.

The H-1B collapse reflects a policy fight, not just screening. A September executive order imposed a $100,000 fee on petitions for newly hired H-1B workers outside the United States; the Department of Homeland Security says filings dropped 91% for workers targeted by the fee. A district court struck the fee down as an unconstitutional tax, but the president issued a new $100,000 fee proclamation in September 2026, and Bier notes that several major companies — including Microsoft, Adobe and Infosys — have been suspended from sponsoring H-1B workers for green cards.

The country-by-country winners and losers

The steepest declines came in countries covered by the administration's restrictions. Immigrant visas for Cubans fell from 2,287 in February 2024 to 64 in February 2026; Pakistan went from 1,981 to 63, Nigeria from 1,023 to 59, Ethiopia from 685 to 7 and Ghana from 782 to 3, according to the State Department tables. Across regions, Central Asia suffered the largest fall at 99%, followed by Africa (-89%), Eastern Europe (-84%) and the Middle East (-81%). Immigration from Muslim-majority nations plunged more than 90%.

Asia fared unevenly but was hit across the board: new immigrant visas fell 31% for China, 25% for Japan, 19% for South Korea and 16% for India. Refugee admissions declined about 90% — from 12,518 in December 2024 to 1,341 in March 2026 — and legal asylum entries at southwest border ports fell 99.9%, from almost 40,000 to just 26. Conversely, Canada and Mexico, exempt from the restrictions, saw immigrant visa issuance rise 142% and 17% respectively.

What it means for Indian applicants

India was not included in the bans or the 75-country immigrant visa pause imposed January 21, 2026 — which federal courts in two cases ordered lifted in August, though most affected applicants are still awaiting visas, the New York Times reported. The 16% fall in immigrant visas for Indians reflects tighter screening, fee changes and the broader slowdown rather than a country-specific freeze.

The practical advice for applicants: employment-based green card pathways remain the steadiest channel, while family reunification routes face longer waits and student and temporary work visas face both fees and stricter adjudication. Anyone planning applications should verify current requirements and restrictions on the State Department's monthly visa statistics page and its immigrant visa processing updates before making plans.

What happens next

The policies were introduced by executive action without congressional approval and face ongoing legal challenges — the August court orders restoring visa issuance in the two cases show the restrictions are not settled law. Bier's broader arithmetic underscores the scale: the cuts to legal immigration amount to the largest since the Hoover administration of 1929–1933, excluding the COVID-19 period, and he calculates that 73% of all entry cuts came from legal, not illegal, immigration.

For the diaspora, the February figures are the last published month — the State Department has not released monthly visa data since February 2026. Until new tables arrive, the trajectory of family reunification, the diversity lottery's fate and the H-1B fee litigation remain the three things to watch.
